points: Vitamin C is water-soluble and is destroyed by oxidation, so cutting exposes more surface to air and causes greater loss.
Soaking, or leaving prepared vegetables standing in water, lets water-soluble vitamins and minerals leach out.
Washing before cutting prevents losses of soluble nutrients that would occur if cut pieces were washed.
Large pieces lose fewer nutrients than small pieces because less surface is exposed to water and air.
A sharp knife or peeler removes less tissue and causes less cell damage than a blunt tool.
Peeling thinly, or leaving edible skins on, keeps nutrients that lie just under the skin, such as vitamin C in potatoes.
Vegetables should be prepared just before cooking to limit the time nutrients are exposed to air and water.
Vitamin C is destroyed by heat and oxidation, and it is lost into cooking water, especially with prolonged boiling.
Water-soluble B vitamins, including thiamine, riboflavin and folate, leach into cooking water and are reduced by prolonged heat.
Carotene is fat-soluble and stable to heat, so it is not lost into cooking water.
Bicarbonate of soda keeps vegetables green, but it destroys vitamin C and softens texture.
Copper and brass pans speed up the destruction of vitamin C; stainless steel or enamel pans should be used instead.
Long cooking gives a poor flavour and nutrient content, while short cooking in minimum water keeps most nutrients.

notes.h: Effects of cooking on colour, texture and flavour
points: Green colour comes from chlorophyll, which turns olive-brown when vegetables are overcooked or cooked in an acid medium, forming pheophytin.
Red cabbage contains anthocyanin pigments that turn blue-green in alkaline conditions and red in acid conditions.
Carotenoid pigments such as beta-carotene remain stable, so orange and red vegetables keep their colour in cooking.
Heat softens the cellulose and pectin in cell walls, so overcooked vegetables become mushy.
Starch in potatoes and pulses gelatinises when heated in water: the granules swell and absorb water, softening the food.
Volatile flavour compounds escape in steam, so flavour is lost during prolonged boiling.
Roasting or frying natural sugars in onions and carrots causes caramelisation, which improves flavour.
Overcooked cabbage and other brassicas release sulphur compounds, which produce a strong, unpleasant odour.
Boiling: cook in the minimum amount of boiling water in a saucepan with a tight-fitting lid, for the minimum time.
Steaming: vegetables cook in steam above boiling water, so fewer nutrients leach away than in boiling water.
Microwaving: a short cooking time with very little water retains much of the vitamin C.
Stir-frying: small pieces cooked quickly in a little oil keep their colour, crispness and vitamins; fat-soluble vitamins are absorbed from the oil.
Frozen vegetables should be cooked from frozen without thawing, to avoid losses in the drip liquid.
Vegetables should be served immediately and kept slightly crisp, since nutrients continue to be lost during holding.
Cooking liquid is kept and used in soups, sauces or gravy so that the dissolved nutrients are eaten.
Blanching: vegetables are briefly immersed in boiling water and then cooled rapidly in cold water.
Blanching before freezing denatures enzymes, fixes bright colour and reduces the number of micro-organisms on the surface.
Blanching causes some loss of water-soluble vitamins, but this is necessary before freezing.
Fruit is often eaten raw to keep its vitamin C; cooked fruit loses more vitamin C than raw fruit.
Stewed fruit should be cooked in a small amount of water with a lid, for a short time, to limit vitamin C loss and keep its texture.
Apples and pears keep more fibre and nutrients when the skin is left on or peeled thinly.
Cut fruit browns through enzymic oxidation; acidic juice such as lemon juice slows browning and helps to keep colour in fruit salads.

keyTerms.definition: A vitamin, such as vitamin C or a B vitamin, that dissolves in water and is lost into cooking water or drip liquid.
A vitamin, such as vitamin A, D, E or K, that dissolves in fat and is not lost into cooking water.
The loss of soluble nutrients and minerals from food into the water used to wash, soak or cook it.
Brief immersion of vegetables in boiling water followed by rapid cooling, to prepare them for freezing.
The swelling of starch granules in hot water, which softens the food and makes starch digestible.
The browning and flavour change that occurs when natural sugars are heated strongly.
The green pigment in vegetables, which changes to an olive-brown colour when overcooked or cooked in acid.
Cooked until still slightly firm to the bite, which keeps texture and reduces nutrient loss.

factCards.term: Four cooking methods that retain most nutrients
factCards.definition: Steaming, microwaving, stir-frying and boiling in the minimum amount of water with a lid.

factCards.term: Why bicarbonate of soda should not be added to vegetable cooking water
factCards.definition: It destroys vitamin C and softens the texture, although it keeps the vegetables green.

factCards.term: Three purposes of blanching before freezing
factCards.definition: Denatures enzymes, fixes bright colour, and reduces micro-organisms on the surface.

factCards.term: Three causes of vitamin C loss in cooking
factCards.definition: Heat, oxidation and leaching into cooking water.
Carotene is fat-soluble and stable to heat, so it is not lost into cooking water.

factCards.term: Colour change of chlorophyll in acid
factCards.definition: Chlorophyll converts to pheophytin, turning the vegetable olive-brown.

factCards.term: Starch change in potatoes on heating
factCards.definition: Gelatinisation: starch granules swell and absorb water, softening the potato.

factCards.term: Why copper and brass pans are avoided for vegetables
factCards.definition: They speed up the destruction of vitamin C during cooking.

questions.prompt: State two reasons why vegetables should be prepared shortly before they are cooked.
questions.model: Any two: cutting exposes more surface to air, so vitamin C is oxidised and destroyed; standing in water or soaking lets water-soluble vitamins and minerals leach out; enzymes and browning reactions begin once cells are damaged.

questions.prompt: Explain how preparation and cooking affect the nutritive value, colour, texture and flavour of green vegetables, and recommend a method of cooking that keeps most of their nutrients.
questions.model: Nutritive value: vitamin C is lost through cutting, soaking, heat, oxidation and leaching into cooking water; water-soluble B vitamins and folate leach out and are reduced by prolonged heat. Colour: chlorophyll turns olive-brown with overcooking or in acid, and bicarbonate of soda keeps green colour only by destroying vitamin C. Texture: heat softens cellulose and pectin, so overcooked vegetables become mushy. Flavour: volatile compounds escape in steam and sulphur compounds in brassicas produce strong odours when overcooked. Recommended method: wash before cutting, prepare just before cooking, use large pieces, then steam, microwave or stir-fry, or boil in the minimum water with a tight lid for the minimum time, serve immediately and use any cooking liquid in soups or sauces.
